thread_analysis.thread_summary: Alinco (contact Mitsunori Kirimoto, with firmware support from outsourced vendor Omnibit/Kosaka) engages Allion (Masaya Iida, Toshitaka Mochizuki, Itsuo Sakai, lab engineer Kenichi Ushiroebisu) for RF/RF PHY and Direct Test Mode testing of the XE1177 product (the same product covered in thread_0016's earlier Class 1/Class 2 BlueTest3 default-configuration dispute) using a Qualcomm chipset and the BlueTest3/TRBI200/QDART tool stack, spanning July through at least mid-October 2025. The thread documents BlueTest3 setup troubleshooting, a Qualcomm-license-restricted DTM tool requirement, an efficient test-sequencing strategy for a Power-Class-ambiguous chipset, an extended firmware power-save-mode misdiagnosis saga, and a parallel test-system-side hardware fault (a degraded GPIB-over-Ethernet connector) that briefly created genuine internal disagreement about whether it was actually DUT-caused before being traced to a physical connector problem on the lab's own equipment.
all_questions_found: Which BlueTest3 Transport option to select, and why does 'Establish connection to OUT' fail after successful DUT mode entry? (see thread_0012_case_01)
Why is a Qualcomm-license-restricted tool (QDART) needed for RF PHY Direct Test Mode, beyond BlueTest3? (see thread_0012_case_02)

Is the test sample's mid-test disconnection a hardware power instability issue requiring a replacement sample, or something else -- and how to verify firmware fix attempts efficiently? (see thread_0012_case_03)

Is an intermittent 'signal analyzer initialization failed' error caused by the customer's firmware, or something else -- and what is the actual confirmed root cause once internal disagreement about attribution was resolved? (see thread_0012_case_04)

How should RF PHY testing be sequenced for a chipset whose existing registration predates the Core Specification's Class 1/Class 2 distinction, to avoid unnecessary full-suite testing? (see thread_0012_case_05)

(Administrative, not separately cased) Software/tool delivery logistics (Blue Suite installer size, duplicate email/password delivery confusion, file naming uncertainty), scheduling and on-site visit coordination, and email distribution-list housekeeping -- routine project administration without a generalizable technical lesson.
thread_analysis.key_technical_discussion: The thread's standout technical contribution is case_03's diagnostic methodology for distinguishing genuine hardware power instability from firmware power-management interference based on dropout timing patterns, paired with a practical LED-based heuristic for provisionally verifying firmware fix attempts. Case_04, substantially enriched in this redo pass, now also models how to handle a genuine internal disagreement about fault attribution: a test engineer's plausible correlation-based argument (reference DUT never shows the error, customer's DUT does) was taken seriously, investigated by re-checking the actual log timeline and identifying a confound (RF vs. RF PHY logs differ in what they record), and only then resolved -- with the final root cause turning out to be a degraded hardware connector on the lab's own test system, confirmed by physical cleaning. Case_05 captures a distinct, generalizable test-efficiency lesson: when a chipset's Power Class is genuinely ambiguous due to registration history, test the cheapest single discriminating item before committing to a full test suite.
thread_analysis.key_decision_logic: See thread_0012_case_01 through thread_0012_case_05 for case-specific decision logic; the throughline is careful root-cause isolation (RF/antenna-path vs. serial/control-path; hardware vs. firmware; DUT-side vs. test-system-side, including genuine internal disagreement about that attribution) before recommending a remediation path or test strategy.
thread_analysis.risk_if_done_wrong: See individual case files; the highest-risk item is case_03, where misattributing firmware-power-save-induced dropouts to a hardware defect could have led to unproductive replacement-sample requests. Case_04 illustrates a more subtle risk: dismissing a team member's correlation-based counter-argument without re-checking the log timeline could have caused a genuine DUT-side effect (had one existed) to be overlooked, while accepting it uncritically could have caused an unsubstantiated claim to reach the customer's firmware vendor.
thread_analysis.consulting_mistake: The initial framing of the dropout issue to the customer as simple 'unstable power' (before the timing-pattern analysis was done) understandably led the customer to first assume a hardware defect and ask about sample replacement. The underlying power-save mode issue also remained unresolved across multiple firmware revisions through the end of the visible thread, ultimately requiring in-person escalation. This redo pass also found that the original case_04 write-up had presented the test-system-vs-DUT fault attribution as a settled, one-message conclusion, when in fact it was genuinely contested internally for several more messages before being resolved -- the original version was accurate as far as it went but omitted the actual epistemic process (re-checking logs, identifying confounds, escalating to the test system vendor, and the eventual physical-hardware root cause) that resolved the disagreement.
thread_analysis.consulting_takeaway: When a test sample's connection drops mid-test, examine the timing pattern of repeated failures before characterizing the issue to the customer as a hardware defect. When multiple distinct fault types surface during an extended multi-round troubleshooting effort, maintain careful attribution discipline so unrelated issues aren't relayed to or conflated by the customer's firmware vendor -- and when a team member raises a plausible counter-argument to an established attribution, investigate it on the actual evidence (log timelines, confounds) rather than either dismissing it or accepting it on correlation alone. Separately, when a chipset's applicable Power Class test suite is ambiguous due to registration history, test the cheapest discriminating item first rather than committing to the full suite upfront.
